intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spondylometaphyseal dysplasia of the Sedaghatian type (SMDS) is caused by compound heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the GPX4 gene.

checks.claim: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia of the Sedaghatian type (SMDS) is caused by compound heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the GPX4 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Our identification of truncating mutations in GPX4 in two families affected with SSMD supports the pathogenic role of mutated GPX4 in this very rare disease.
checks.explanation: Compound heterozygosity is shown in one family. Homozygosity is only implied: both parents carried the same heterozygous stop mutation, but the affected child's DNA was not available.

paragraphs.text: Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia is a neonatal lethal form of spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. Its features are severe metaphyseal chondrodysplasia with mild limb shortening, platyspondyly, cardiac conduction defects, and central nervous system abnormalities (summary by Smith et al., 2014).

paragraphs.text: Sedaghatian (1980) reported 2 brothers, born within a year of each other, who had severe congenital metaphyseal involvement, mild rhizomelic shortness of the upper limbs, and mild platyspondyly. Both died at 3 days of age of cardiorespiratory insufficiency. Only one had antemortem laboratory tests. These showed low calcium, high phosphorus, and high alkaline phosphatase, which were attributed to a renal defect. At autopsy, the same infant had pulmonary, renal, and adrenal hemorrhage, as well as subendocardial myocarditis and myocardial necrosis. The parents were normal and had recently had an affected daughter.

paragraphs.text: Opitz et al. (1987) described a second Iranian family. The affected infant died on day 4, and histology showed severe epimetaphyseal dysplasia. The authors noted that one of Sedaghatian's patients also had microphthalmia, asymmetric ears, a depressed nasal bridge, a broad nose, a short neck, a prominent sternum, and short lower extremities. They suggested that the syndrome may be more complexly pleiotropic than the radiographs indicate.

paragraphs.text: English et al. (2006) reported a female infant with SMDS born to nonconsanguineous Caucasian parents. She was hypotonic from birth and had recurrent cyanotic episodes within a few hours of delivery. Cerebral imaging showed absence of the corpus callosum and marked frontotemporal pachygyria. She developed seizures on day 14 of life and died at 17 days of age. The authors suggested that neuronal migration abnormalities can occur in SMDS and proposed a novel association with agenesis of the corpus callosum.

paragraphs.text: Sedaghatian (1980) presumed autosomal recessive inheritance because the parents were normal and had affected children of both sexes. Opitz et al. (1987) reported an affected infant born to first-cousin parents. They also noted that all known cases at that time were Iranian, and suggested that SMDS is an autosomal recessive trait with a high gene frequency in Iranians.

checks.evidence_quote: since parents are normal and recently had an affected baby girl, it is presumed that this disorder is an autosomal recessive trait.
checks.explanation: The affected children were two brothers and a girl, so both sexes were affected, and the paper bases its presumption of autosomal recessive inheritance on this. 'SMDS' is the standard name for the disorder the paper describes.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2014) performed whole-exome sequencing in a girl with SMDS and her unaffected parents. The girl was compound heterozygous for 2 rare variants in the GPX4 gene (NM_001039848.1), both predicted to affect splicing. The first, c.587+5G-A, was inherited from the mother. The second, c.588-8_588-4del, had arisen de novo. In vitro studies showed that the first mutation caused part of exon 4 to be spliced out and the second caused skipping of exon 5. Both led to a frameshift and premature truncation of GPX4. In a second, unrelated family, DNA from the affected child was not available. Sanger sequencing showed that both unaffected parents carried the same heterozygous stop mutation in exon 3 of GPX4, c.381C-A (Y127X).

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2014) used whole-exome sequencing to study a girl with SMDS. They found a c.587+5G-A mutation in the GPX4 gene (NM_001039848.1), inherited from her mother. The girl was compound heterozygous for this mutation and a de novo 5-bp deletion (c.588-8_588-4del). In vitro studies showed that the c.587+5G-A mutation caused part of exon 4 to be spliced out, leading to a frameshift and premature truncation of GPX4.
